summary.en: Mixed conditionals join a condition and a result that belong to **different times**. The most common pattern links an unreal past with a present result: _If I **had taken** that job, I **would be** living in Lisbon now._ The other links an unreal present or permanent situation with a past result: _If she **were** more careful, she **wouldn't have lost** the keys._ Time words such as _now_, _today_, _still_ and _yesterday_ show which time each half refers to.
summary.es: Se mezclan los tiempos porque la condición y el resultado no coinciden en el tiempo: «si hubiera aceptado (entonces), ahora viviría en Lisboa».

form: Past condition → present result: **if** + past perfect, **would / could / might** + infinitive
Present or general condition → past result: **if** + past simple, **would / could / might** + **have** + past participle
Time words show the switch: _now, today, these days, still_ (present); _then, last year, at the time_ (past)
Negative forms are common: _If I hadn't missed the flight, I'd still be on holiday._

uses.text: **A past decision with a present consequence**: _If we had bought the flat in 2015, we would own it outright by now._
**A personality trait or permanent fact with a past consequence**: _If he weren't so stubborn, he would have accepted our help._
**Reflecting on turning points in your life**, useful in Speaking part 4: _If I hadn't studied abroad, my English wouldn't be this fluent._

mistakes.wrong: If I would have saved more, I would own a flat now.
mistakes.right: If I had saved more, I would own a flat now.

why.en: Would never goes in the if clause; use the past perfect.
why.es: No pongas would en la parte con if: usa had + participio.

mistakes.wrong: If I were more organised, I wouldn't miss the deadline yesterday.
mistakes.right: If I were more organised, I wouldn't have missed the deadline yesterday.

why.en: A result in the past needs would have + past participle.
why.es: Un resultado en el pasado pide would have + participio.

mistakes.wrong: If I would be taller, I would have joined the police.
mistakes.right: If I were taller, I would have joined the police.

why.en: The unreal present in the if clause is past simple (were), not would be.
why.es: En la parte con if va were, no would be.

examples.en: If I had taken that job in Madrid, I would be living there now.
If she had listened to the doctor, she wouldn't be in so much pain today.
examples.es: Si hubiera hecho caso al médico, hoy no tendría tanto dolor.

examples.en: If we hadn't missed the flight, we would still be on holiday.
If the company had invested in training, its staff would be far more productive now.
If I hadn't studied abroad, my English wouldn't be this fluent.
If he weren't so stubborn, he would have accepted our help last week.
examples.es: Si no fuera tan terco, habría aceptado nuestra ayuda la semana pasada.

examples.en: If I were a more patient person, I wouldn't have lost my temper at the meeting.
If she spoke better Italian, she might have got the job in Milan.
If the roads were safer, fewer people would have died last winter.
If it hadn't been for my brother's advice, I would still be unhappy at work.

practice.prompt: If I ___ that email last night, I wouldn't be in trouble now.

explanation.en: Past condition (last night) with a present result (now): past perfect in the if clause.

practice.prompt: If she weren't so stubborn, she ___ our advice last week.

explanation.en: A general trait (weren't) with a past result (last week): would have + past participle.

practice.prompt: If the company ___ the new software in 2019, it would be far more efficient today.

explanation.en: In 2019 is past, so the if clause takes the past perfect; today needs would be.

practice.prompt: If I ___ a naturally shy person, I would have spoken up at yesterday's meeting.

explanation.en: An unreal general fact takes past simple (were) in the if clause, never would.

practice.prompt: We would still be waiting for a table if we ___ a booking yesterday.

explanation.en: Yesterday is past, so the if clause uses the past perfect; the result (still waiting) is present.
